mutant.description: AC1's whole oracle is the EXIT CODE of `git merge-base --is-ancestor`, a one-bit instrument whose PASS value is rc=0 -- the same value a great many git invocations return for reasons unrelated to ancestry. An instrument that can only ever print the passing value proves nothing, and that failure mode is invisible because the answer looks right. The planted condition is therefore a pair of objects for which the true answer is NO.
mutant.expected: The identical command, with the two commit arguments REVERSED so that the true answer is 'no', must return rc=1 rather than rc=0. If it returns 0 both ways the instrument is not reading ancestry and AC1's PASS is void.
mutant.observed: FIRED. `git merge-base --is-ancestor b0b65368fb HEAD; echo rc=$?` prints rc=0; `git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD b0b65368fb; echo rc=$?` prints rc=1. Two further live readings in the same family discriminate in both directions, so the one-bit oracle is exercised across four calls and not two: origin/CLOUD @78c1e121d2 as an ancestor of HEAD reads rc=0, and the push-state sweep's reversed control (origin/box/sitez @84da5399cf as a descendant test against 4b8e5e530a) reads rc=1. THE STRONGEST CONTROL IS HISTORICAL AND IS NOT MINE TO RE-RUN: before the merge the same command on the same two objects read rc=1, recorded in this order's step 1 as 'merge-base --is-ancestor b0b65368fb HEAD = rc 1' across all three attempts. So the bit FLIPPED across the act, which is the only form in which a one-bit PASS carries information.
